stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, public domain (abridged); photograph: raising the American flag at the Government House, Honolulu, August 12, 1898, public domain.
stimulus.text: "Article I. Spain relinquishes all claim of sovereignty over and title to Cuba. Article II. Spain cedes to the United States the island of Porto Rico and other islands now under Spanish sovereignty in the West Indies, and the island of Guam in the Marianas or Ladrones. Article III. Spain cedes to the United States the archipelago known as the Philippine Islands. . . ." — Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898 (abridged). Background from the books: the United States agreed to pay Spain $20 million for the Philippine Islands.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from the Treaty of Paris, December 10, 1898, public domain, with a public-domain 1898 photograph
stem: The treaty gave the United States the Philippines, an island chain thousands of miles away with millions of people. That fact best explains why the treaty

options.text: Was signed in Paris before the war with Spain began
options.misconception: The treaty was signed in December 1898, after the fighting ended in August.

options.text: Set off the fiercest debate over annexation in the Senate

options.misconception: Article III cedes the Philippines to the United States; it does not free them.
The Senate ratified the treaty in February 1899, though by a narrow margin.

rationales.A: The treaty was signed in December 1898, after the armistice of August. It ended the war, it did not precede it.
rationales.B: Background from the books: keeping a distant, populous archipelago split the Senate, and ratification was nearly quashed.
rationales.C: Article III hands the Philippines to the United States. Freedom was what the Filipinos then had to fight for.
rationales.D: The Senate ratified the treaty in February 1899. The vote was close, but the treaty passed.
rationales.general:
1. Measure the prize. The Philippines are thousands of miles away, crowded with people who never asked for American rule.
2. Ask what that meant. Keeping them meant America would rule a colony, not free a neighbor.
3. Follow the fight. That question split the Senate, and ratification nearly failed.
Remember: the size of a prize changes the argument about it, so ask what the new territory would force the country to become.
